models.purpose: grade a city's smart growth on one number
models.summary: The Smart Growth Index is the sum of five metrics, each scored from 0 to 20, so the whole index runs from 0 to 100. The five are weighed evenly because each was taken to matter the same.

variables.definition: the sum of the five metric scores, on a scale of 0 to 100

governing_equations.label: smart growth index
governing_equations.source_expression: SGI=Smart\ Land\ Use+Smart\ Community+Smart\ Development+Smart\ Housing+Smart\ Transportation
governing_equations.normalized_latex: SGI=Smart\ Land\ Use+Smart\ Community+Smart\ Development+Smart\ Housing+Smart\ Transportation
governing_equations.purpose: the index is the unweighted sum of the five metrics, each scored out of 20

equation_status.reason: displayed and read from the page

objectives: give a city one number that can be compared with another

details: the index is computed from the current data for each city

parameter_estimation.method: equal weights are assumed rather than fitted

algorithm.convergence_criteria: the sum is written out and the cap of 20 per metric is stated

assumptions: equal weights are the right default
the grading scale is the familiar one

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: the sum and the 0 to 100 scale are both printed

validation_refs: the equation is set off on its own line
strengths: the scale is stated before the algebra
the cap makes the index readable
limitations: equal weights are assumed, and the paper later says this may not hold
improving one metric alone can raise the index
missing_details: no test of the equal weights is given

models.purpose: score mixed use and open space together
models.summary: Land use averages two ratios. Population density is divided by the densest city in the region, and park area per 1000 residents is divided by the largest such area found. Los Angeles and Glasgow set the density ceilings; Honolulu sets the park ceiling.

variables.definition: the highest population density found in the region
the largest park area per 1000 people used as the normalizer

governing_equations.label: smart land use
governing_equations.purpose: density and park area, each divided by a regional maximum, then averaged

equation_status.reason: displayed and read from the page

objectives: reward compact building and preserved open space in one score
constraints: higher density means more people in vertical buildings
the regional maximum is the right normalizer

details: the normalizers are fixed before the city is scored

parameter_estimation.method: the normalizers are taken from published city data

steps: divide each measure by its regional maximum
algorithm.convergence_criteria: the formula and its four symbols are printed

assumptions: density stands in for mixed use
park area stands in for open space

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: the formula is printed, but the normalizer is described two ways

validation_refs: the equation is set off on its own line
strengths: both normalizers are named and sourced
limitations: the prose calls the park normalizer a median while the formula labels it a maximum
density near business zones also raises housing cost, which the metric ignores
missing_details: no rule fixes which city counts as the regional maximum

models.purpose: stand in for pride of place with crime and the budget
models.summary: The community score averages a crime index with the share of the budget spent on restoration and maintenance rather than new construction. The paper calls both choices rough, and says crime is sometimes a matter of survival rather than a lack of pride.

variables.definition: share of the city budget spent on restoration and maintenance
money spent on restoration and maintenance

governing_equations.label: community metric
governing_equations.purpose: the average of the crime index and the remediation share of the budget

governing_equations.label: remediation share
governing_equations.purpose: the remediation share written out as a ratio of the two budget figures

equation_status.reason: displayed and read from the page

objectives: put a number on a sense of place
constraints: a low crime index means residents feel safe
restoration spending counts as developing existing communities

details: the budget is classified for the current year

parameter_estimation.method: both inputs are read from published sources

algorithm.convergence_criteria: the formula and the budget ratio are both printed

assumptions: crime is the closest available stand-in for pride
the budget split can be read by hand

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: both the average and the budget ratio are printed

validation_refs: the equation is set off on its own line
strengths: the paper names the shortcut and its weakness
the budget categories that count are listed
limitations: crime does not always signal pride

missing_details: no check on the hand classification is offered

models.purpose: score engagement, fairness and renewable intent
models.summary: Development averages four terms: country transparency, city voter turnout, the projected renewable share, and one minus the poverty rate. Transparency is the only input taken at country level rather than city level, and renewables sit outside the ten principles the rest of the model is built on.

variables.definition: government transparency score for the country
share of the population that votes
share of the population below the poverty line

governing_equations.label: development metric
governing_equations.purpose: transparency, turnout and renewables raise the score and poverty lowers it

equation_status.reason: displayed and read from the page

objectives: capture engagement and fairness in one score
constraints: a rising renewable share shows good intentions

details: the four inputs are taken from the most recent year available

parameter_estimation.method: the four inputs are read from published sources

algorithm.convergence_criteria: the formula and all four symbols are printed

assumptions: country transparency is a fair stand-in for city developers
renewables belong in the score even though no principle names them
validation_refs: the equation is set off on its own line
strengths: the extra measure is flagged as sitting outside the ten principles

limitations: the prose says three measures were used and then lists four

missing_details: no city-level corruption figure is used

models.purpose: score the range of housing from ownership and homelessness
models.summary: Housing averages the share of owner-occupied homes minus the homeless share. The paper treats the link from ownership to housing range as a large simplifying assumption, and warns that the metric could reward gentrification if the development score is low.

variables.definition: share of residences that are owner occupied
homeless population as a share of the city

governing_equations.label: housing metric
governing_equations.purpose: ownership raises the score and homelessness lowers it

constraints: more owners means more housing options
a larger homeless share means the range is too narrow

parameter_estimation.method: both inputs are read from published sources

algorithm.convergence_criteria: the formula and both symbols are printed

assumptions: every working group is needed in a city

strengths: the paper flags the assumption and the gentrification risk in the same paragraph

models.purpose: score transport by what people use, not what is offered
models.summary: Transportation averages the share of commuters on public transit and the share who walk. Cycling and carpooling are left out for lack of data, and the paper argues that use, rather than what is merely offered, shows whether a city has succeeded in promoting alternatives.

variables.definition: share of commuters using public transportation

governing_equations.label: transportation metric
governing_equations.purpose: the average of the public transit share and the walking share
